utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, could we have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can you bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is going to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please sit down. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the Trial Chamber has granted the protective measures that you have requested, which means that your image will be distorted and also your voice will be distorted and you will be referred to by a pseudonym. The usher now will show you a piece of paper which has your name on it and your pseudonym, and if you will just look at it and confirm that it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: As you will see on the sheet of paper, you will be referred to as Witness XX. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, for the first part of my examination, I would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, what happened on the 9th of May, 1993? Where were you and what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, I was at home with my family, with my wife and my daughter, and early in the morning, we were awakened by intense explosions and shooting. Shortly after that, we heard on the radio a statement by Jadranko Topic, called Cela, who stated that there was a coordinated operation of the HVO underway which will be over soon and that all the Bosniaks should hoist a white cloth as a sign of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you stated that you were at home. Was your house at that time in West or East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: In the west side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, did this attack by the HVO, did this come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, for the period of time, one could feel that something could happen, but I really did not expect something of -- anything of that proportion. Otherwise, I would not have been there. I would have taken my family, and also I would have gone myself somewhere, where it was safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that a man named Jadranko Topic was on the radio asking the Bosnians to actually put white cloths outside of the window. First of all, who is Jadranko Topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, Jadranko Topic at that time was a high official in the HDZ. I don't know his exact office, but one could say that he was the HDZ's political figure number 1 in the town, at least as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you follow the requests -- well, the request he made on the radio to actually put a white sheet out of the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, no. I thought that if I put out any piece of white cloth, it would draw attention to me and my family. And that in that case, perhaps my lot would have -- might be worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you or any of your family members go out that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: No. I dared not go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you find out whether any of your relatives who were also living in that neighbourhood, did you find out what happened to them on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I didn't, at first, and we were very worried because both my wife and I -- that is relatives of both my wife's and mine lived in the western part of the town, and we didn't know what was going on. However, a Croat friend of ours came to us and told us that my folk had started -- that they were about to be detained, but that they had found shelter with somebody else. However, my wife realised that some of her relatives were gone, and her younger brother, too, that he was missing, and she returned crying, and later on we found out that her mother and her younger brother - and he was underage - had been taken to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know how long they had to stay there in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I think about a week, but after that, they dared not return to their flat, and instead tried to manage with other relatives, hiding with them. I'm talking about my mother-in-law and her son. My mother and father were also there for a while, and they returned to their flat. That is, they were hiding with their neighbours. Their neighbours helped them and shielded them, and a few days later, when the situation calmed down somewhat, they went back to their flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, what did you do in the days following the 9th of May attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I dared not go out anywhere. I feared for my family and myself. And I didn't know what was really going on. But so my family and I were in the flat, fearful, waiting for somebody to come and take us. Whenever we would hear some sound or something, we would panic and start dressing quickly, because we thought that my daughter, my wife, might be expelled and that I might be taken to prison or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did, in this period, actually people try to get into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Several times somebody came to the doors of my flat, but we also had some good neighbours, Croats. And one of those neighbours, several times, twice, I think, prevented them because he was also a member of the HVO. So he would go down the stairs and tell those people to go away. On one occasion, some people who were drunk or maybe under drugs who came to the doors and he asked -- and they wanted to ask me if I was with the civil defence and then [redacted], told them that they had nothing to look there for, and that they should go away, and they did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters have requested if you could slow down your pace a little bit so they can interpret more easily, and I would request if that name can be redacted from the transcript. Witness, try to refrain from mentioning any names unless I specifically ask you to mention names, if you could. Witness, what happened on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, 1993, there were all around arrests or, rather, all people with Muslim, that is Bosniak names, were arrested. At that time, there was fierce conflict between the BH army and the HVO. That was at the time when the BH army had taken Bijelo Polje and the northern camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you also arrested on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes. We all panicked. At home, my wife and daughter were crying. Like other neighbours, that is, people who were Muslims, Bosniaks in that same building, I was arrested and taken to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what happened when you arrived at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: When we arrived at the Heliodrom, some of us were put in a school at the Heliodrom in a room. I'm not sure, but I think that we were about 50. And that same evening, two young men came, and they were very young, they could have been around 20. They started to ill-treat the prisoners. I do not know the names. I do not know who they are to this day. One of them entered with a cocked pistol and with this pistol, he circled around the room until he could find somebody, I don't know what was the criterion, and then he would take that person out of the room and that man would be beaten then. I know that two men were beaten in the same way, that is, with a pistol pointing at them, they would be picked out. The third one wasn't beaten because he told them, even though he was a Muslim, he was a member of the HVO, and so they told him to get back into the room, and he wasn't beaten on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you picked out on that evening as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Although, like all the other prisoners, I was really scared because the pistol would go all over all of us and I -- nobody could be sure who would be picked out and who -- and taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This happened on the first evening. Did this happen more often after you -- while you were detained at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: The ill treatment went on, of course not always in the same way. In the school, very often we would be woken up late in the night, sometimes around 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning. We all had to run out of this room, run down the passage while not being allowed to look at the guards, and the guards -- he struck some of us and there was a lot of noise, and at times, when some of those guards were under the influence, they would then force us to sing the Croatian anthem, some Ustasa songs dating back to World War II when we were in this crowd, and that is how they ill-treated us. I also heard that on the ground floor, that is, I was told by prisoners who were on the ground floor that above their heads, and I said late at night when they would be trying to sleep, that they could hear a round of fire, fired above their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a man by the name of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a man by the name of Nenad Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I do or, rather, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is he and how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: May I answer? Are we in a closed session? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We may need to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness XX, how long were you kept in the school building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, in the school building, I think I spent about a month there. After that - and again I do not know on the basis of what criteria - I was transferred to the central prison. I still don't know what were the criteria for this, because in the central prison, there were some elderly men and there was even a boy, an underaged boy, in the same room with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, where were you put in the central prison? Can you describe the room and the persons you -- also the size of the room and the persons 1 you were with in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: That room was about 90 metres square, 90 to 100 metres square. We were about 100 in that room. The conditions were horrible. If we wanted to sleep, we were packed like sardines. If one wanted to turn, everybody had to do that, or if somebody wanted to go to the toilet, he would have to tread on other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many toilets were there for this group of 100 detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: There was only one lavatory, and I can say that all our social life in the prison consisted of washing, cleaning, but at times, we had to wash ourselves by simply pouring water from one other -- from two Coca Cola bottles. We simply could not get to the faucets, to the taps, and that's why there was so many diseases in the prison. I know that once the whole room was vacated and all the prisoners had to be sprayed. I think that on one occasion scabies started to spread, and one man was affected, and he had to be isolated for a while, but then he came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you get for food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: It was very meagre. I lost some 15 kilograms during the first month or so. Of morning, we would get a slice of bread and tea, and for lunch, we were served some mixture, and we most of us couldn't -- I don't think we could guess what that was. I would say those were just some leftovers put and mixed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, how were you treated in the central prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: In the central prison, it was very difficult, especially because next to our room were Croat detainees, that's those who were members of the HVO, but I think they were proper criminals and drug addicts because it often happened, how we, the prisoners, could see them walk past us with the syringes in their hand and go towards the toilets where they were being given shots or taking shots, and it was those prisoners who harassed us most practically. They used to take people out and whatever they still had with them, that is what had not been taken from them, watches or if they had still some money hidden, they would search them and take it. And we were offered no assistance, no help, from people who guarded us. On one occasion, I remember how they threw a blanket into the room which was on fire so the whole room could go on fire, and when we tried to put that fire out, they began to throw some bottles at us. But I remember that the fire -- that blanket went out all by itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the names of these HVO prisoners who were there maltreating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I don't, but I know that one was called Splico - or other people referred to him as Splico - said he was a member of the paramilitary forces or something like that. He came from Split and he was a drug addict. I remember a young man, he was one of them, and why had he been detained, I don't know, but his nickname was Paraga, but I cannot say positively whether he ill-treated anyone. He was near those people who ill-treated us, but I did not see him ill-treat anyone, whereas this young man nicknamed Splico participated very actively in the ill treatment of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you witness any of the maltreatment by Splico, and what did you witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, yes. I can give you one example. Once we went for lunch and those Croats -- those prisoners of Croat ethnicity searched all our belongings, hoping to find something valuable and appropriating it. But what they did was the -- they found identity cards, or rather the papers of two policemen detained there and of the then lawful police of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when we came back from lunch, they looked around, they tried to identify those men on the basis of the photographs. They did in the case of one of them. They could not recognise the other one fortunately, because he had lost too much weight, and besides, some prisoners said that he had left, that he was no longer there. So the one they could identify, they beat him badly, and this young man that I already mentioned, who was nicknamed Splico, was very active in that, and I think that on that occasion, a tooth was knocked out, and he was pretty badly beaten. He was kicked and beaten with fists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one more question on these HVO prisoners. You said that they were in a room adjacent to your room. What were the conditions in the room that they were staying in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Much better than ours, because they all had their own beds, they had sufficient number of blankets, whereas we slept on the floor. Well, some did have something to cover, some didn't. Some had some blankets, some didn't. And I already told you how many of us were kept in that room. I do not know how many of those Croat prisoners there were, but every one of them had his own, had a bed to him, and enough room in that cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did the guards of the Heliodrom do anything to prevent these HVO prisoners of maltreating you and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: No, no. Absolutely nothing. They did absolutely nothing. I even think that those prisoners were prodded to do it, because some other colleagues imprisoned there said that they tried to defend themselves when these ones were about to attack them, but they then shouted and made so much noise and called to guards to -- saying that Muslims were beating Croat prisoners, and then the guards entered and beat them. So they were beaten rather than helped by the guards. I wasn't present on that occasion. I heard that from other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, my really final question on this issue. Could you perhaps describe the man you've been referring to as Splico?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, young. I mean he was young at that time, quite thin, about 185 centimetres tall. I don't think, however, I'd be able to recognise him because -- now because it was a long time ago. I do not know anything else about him. All I know is that that was the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, while you were at the Heliodrom, were you ever taken out for labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes, a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which locations were you taken to when -- what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I was taken to different locations around town, Santiceva Street, mostly along the separation lines or rather along the confrontation lines between the HVO and the BH army, Santiceva Street, Bulevar, then next to what used to be the department store, Hit department store, but it burnt down. Then I was taken to the Buna, Laksevine, to Hodbina, that is to different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you, in general, describe the type of work you had to do in these places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, by and large we were made to dig trenches or make bunkers for the HVO. In this way, it was trying either to hold on to the front line or perhaps advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you've stated that you also worked at the Bulevar. How many times did you work at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, twice, at least. I am not quite sure, but I think it was two or maybe even three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 14.5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, while the -- we get this exhibit, could you tell us if you remember the times that you were taken to the Bulevar; do you remember who took you to the Bulevar from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Mostly, it was the unknown men, members of the HVO in camouflage uniforms. They would enter the room where we were staying and pointed at us and they referred to us as pieces, they said, "We want 20 pieces, 30 pieces." They would just look at us. They were looking to find men who were physically in better shape, even though occasionally they would also take either the elderly or those who were infirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall any names of the persons who actually picked you out and took you to, in this case, to the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I don't remember the persons who were taking us there. For the most part, I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you're going to be shown a photograph which you may want to put on the ELMO after you've had a look at it. What I would like you to do is, first of all, do you recognise this photograph, what's depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I do recognise it. It's the -- it's the Bulevar or the former line of separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, could you please, with the marker, indicate the actual location where you worked when you were working at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this was in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe with the pointer you can also indicate where you made the mark because it may be a bit difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, what was it that you have to do there, that you had to do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: We dug trenches and built bunkers for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you recall any particular incidents or incident while you were working at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, on one occasion, we were used as human shields because the trenches were not dug as well as they should have. The prisoners were told to line up and protect the HVO soldiers who were passing through that trench. And that was one of the incidents, if you can call it an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, in the area where you had to line up, was the area exposed in the sense that the soldiers from the other side of the confrontation line could actually hit you or shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that was exactly the reason for us being lined up in that way because the members of the HVO probably expected that the members of the ABiH would not shoot if they saw prisoners being lined up there because we were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did there -- in fact, was there any shooting while you were lined up there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall for which HVO unit you were working while you were working at the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I don't know the names of units; however, there were different people there indeed who were members of the HVO. I know that there were some persons who had -- I believe that there was a Canadian of Croatian origin, there was one U.S., a dark man, and then there was a German. Some of them also spoke in clear Croatian accent even though they did not wear HV uniforms. For instance, one of them had a clear Dalmatian accent, but I don't know exactly what the units were and what they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the names of the HVO soldiers who were there at the Bulevar while you were working there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I remember. I remember some Bosniaks who were also with the HVO, but for the most part these were men with criminal records. I know that Benito Sesar was around there. I don't know if he was a member, but he was there on one occasion. He came to the confrontation line on one occasion. Senad Mahmutovic was also there. There was also a person named Fadil, I think, Golos, nicknamed Cuni. I know that Senad Mahmutovic had a criminal record. For this Cuni, they said that he was a drug user.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you please spell the name of that last person you've been referring to; is that a nickname or a full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Who are you referring to? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Cuni.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I believe Fadil Golos, as far as I can remember right now. This is a long time ago, but I think it is, first name F-a-d-i-l, last name G-o-l-o-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the nickname of this Fadil Golos was Cuni; am I correct in understanding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes, I believe Cuni, C-u-n-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you also said that you worked at the Santiceva Street. On how many occasions did you work there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: At least twice. Once we were there for three days. We were taken to sleep to the Dzemal Bijedic University, and it was indeed very tough working there, because we were taken there at gunpoint. We were making bunkers and trenches for the HVO soldiers, and they were trying to extend the line facing the ABiH, and also we feared that the ABiH soldiers could also shoot at us because we were going into their territory and building bunkers there. On several occasions, it happened to me that I had warning shots flying near me, because I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you see prisoners get wounded at Santiceva street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I know that one prisoner was wounded when I was around there, because he was carried by me, and I saw him covered in blood. I don't know exactly where he had been hit, but before this, there had been firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, were you on one occasion also taken to Rastani? And when was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I was taken to Rastani sometime around the 15th of September, 1993, also to perform labour, with a group of prisoners. I believe we were about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you have to do and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: First off, I should say that we were guarded by the Protection Platoon, and I have to say that they behaved correctly, but we were also digging trenches there on -- at the confrontation line facing the army, and I believe that on that occasion, one of the prisoners, I don't recall his name now, had to carry mines into the Mostar hydro power plant. They were to be deployed there in case that the ABiH decided to move and advance on Rastani.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did the ABiH in fact move and advance into Rastani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I think that that was on the 20th. And on that occasion, I was set free with -- along with this group of prisoners who were working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, what did you do when you were set free in Rastani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: We were there for a period of time, and then we crossed over to the free territory. However, Rastani were counterattacked a day later and retaken by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- when the -- when there was a counterattack again by the HVO, whether there were any prisoners involved in this counterattack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Later on, I heard that some prisoners had been pushed in front of the HVO troops during the attack and that some of them were killed. I don't know any names, but I know that on that occasion, some of those prisoners managed to escape, that is to cross over to the free territory, two persons whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you -- when you were set free, did you return to East Mostar? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for my last couple of questions, I'd like to go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll have our break, about 25 minutes. We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are we going to have our witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I can make use of one moment. The most important thing of course, at least I think so, is to finish the witness as far as possible, and so if we can use that time to do so, that would be my preference. But I did, as I said I would, I do have with me the statements about the wooden rifles and photographs of the wooden rifle, and we can either do that if we have time yet tonight or we can do it in the morning, but I do want to make the Chamber, since I represented to you that I would do it today, that it is available and if we have time, we can do it this evening or we can do it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do that after we finish with this testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down, Witness. Any cross-examination? Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I am Zelimir Par, and I am one of the Defence attorneys for Mr. Vinko Martinovic. I'm going to ask you a few questions in relation to your evidence today. Please, can you tell me, do you still work in the same job that you said you had worked on previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I think that this was done in the closed session. I don't know if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We are in the open session, but I think you can say this now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were you involved in any activities in trying to determine the cause of death of Nenad Harmandic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Personally, I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can go into the private session just in case something comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Who received you at the Heliodrom personally? I mean who was that, which organisation? Was it the army? Was it the military police? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: What I know is that those men had HVO uniform on, camouflage uniforms. They were the ones who took us in and -- who took us to and into the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And at the Heliodrom itself, there were some men who brought you there and others received you there. Those who received you, you say that they had HVO uniforms. Did they have white belts? Could you perhaps say if they were military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly if there were any white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And did you generally, during your stay at the Heliodrom, did you see those guards wear any white belts? Or rather, could you see if the Heliodrom was being manned, was being run, by the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: From time to time, I saw men who I could assume were military policemen, but who they were exactly, I wouldn't really know. They were guards there. They were prison guards, I do not really know what to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, who was it that took your names down? Or did anyone register you when you arrived at the Heliodrom? When you arrived you were then registered by somebody. What was done next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Yes, all our names were taken down. We were made to stand in a line, and all our names were taken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But my question was who did that? What did that person look like? What are the circumstances, the impression you got? I can't really make any guesses. Would you tell me what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, those persons wore camouflage uniforms. I know the names of some of them. They were there at the time when the names were being taken down. I do not know exactly who it was that registered my name, but I know some of the men who were present there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No, I'm not interested in specific persons, I'm interested in the procedure. You arrived where your name is taken down. What happens, how does it go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Nobody told us why our names were being taken down or why we were there. Well, perhaps I could have understood because I was a member of the police, for that reason. But as I told you, people were rounded up from the buildings. I mean all the Bosniaks, regardless, and there were people who -- I should say that the majority of them were not active in any formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that, and we heard it in your testimony and in the testimony of others, but what we are talking about now is not the criteria on the basis of which they were brought there, but what was the procedure? Who was in command? Do you know who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: No, I do not know that. I know that one person on one occasion mentioned that he knew who that was but I just don't recall the name, that he knew who was the warden there, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You see, I am asking you all this because I think that you are a competent person in this regard because you found yourself in a situation where you could observe, see, register, certain things better than some others. And I'm asking you so that we could gain a picture from a person who would know how to observe those things, who could see who was doing what, who were the persons doing that. Was it the military police? Was it a prison? Was it a camp? Whether there was some internal organisation or something, in that sense, I meant if you could help us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, I do not know if you think that I am more competent than others to answer that. I think, however, that first of all, I was very much afraid, and that I feared for my life all the time so that perhaps now, if something happened -- if something like that happened to me again, perhaps I would pay more attention to them now than I did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And let's know about this labour duty. You have arrived at the airport [as interpreted], you are there, and they take you. Now, do they take your names down when you come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, they did take no names down. No, they didn't, or at least I didn't see them on some occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Would they take down the names of who has left and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Well, just as I have just told you. As far as I can remember, at times they took our names down, at times they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Why I am asking you this. Now, from the Heliodrom you go to a unit. Do you feel -- do you go on feeling as if you were a prisoner of the Heliodrom or have you become at that moment a prisoner of that unit? Do you think that that is the extended arm of the Heliodrom when you are there? Are you still a Heliodrom prisoner, sent to work as a Heliodrom prisoner to a unit and brought back to those who have power over you, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Believe me, I never gave it a thought at the time. The only thing I thought about was how to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, then. And now, now, you do have any idea, do you have any knowledge about this or not? If not, then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I don't know what the organisation was. I think I understand what you're trying to ask me, but I do not know what was the organisation and who was directly responsible for us, people who kept us there or people who took us away. I really do not know that. I should say both.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Now we are at the Heliodrom, and I'm talking about Harmandic, that part of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a moment, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I won't mention names or places. I only have one question. We can do that, but I just -- yes, let us go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think we should go into private session for this. It's a specific request from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Bulevar. You go to work on the Bulevar. You drew to us a place where you were. You gave us the names of some people who were there. If I noted that down correctly, the names was Benito Sesar, Senad Mahmutcehajic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Senad Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Senad Mahmutovic, Fadil Golos. So my question is: Do you know, have any knowledge, if those persons whose names we have just mentioned ere members of the Benko Penavic's unit commanded by Mario Milicevic, Baja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I do not know what unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we received from the Prosecution information about all these units. But Benko Penavic, the Prosecutor doesn't have it and nobody else gave it for that particular unit, any document, so I cannot show you any of these documents, but be that as it may, you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I do not have any more questions. Your Honours, I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination from Defence counsel for Naletilic? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that my colleague has asked all the questions that the Defence of Mr. Mladen Naletilic may have to ask so that I do not want to waste your time anymore with any cross-examination on our part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if this is something that you know as a citizen of Mostar: If someone makes a complaint about criminal activity against a person on the west side, who investigates that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Right now in Mostar -- are we in a closed session? At present, there are six --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I don't think we are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Regarding your work on the front lines, you told us that you were used as a kind of a wall, as a kind of a screen to protect HVO fighters because the latter thought that the BH army, when they saw you, would abstain from fire because you were wearing civilian clothes. Now, I did not expect you to tell us what the HVO combatants thought when they put you in front of them. What I should like to know, rather, is how did things happen specifically? Were you there to receive the bullets fired by the army across the street or did your presence there actually dissuade the BH army from attacking? What happened? Were you really a screen or what happened, or was it really to prevent others from shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I can say that we were made to be human shields so that they could pass securely. I think that they were expecting the members of the ABiH not to shoot or, if they did shoot, that we would be hit first and then they would have enough time to take cover. I don't know what I thought, but I think that that may have been the line of thinking that they were pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this human shield, this is something that we heard about and this is the first time that we heard that it was a means of dissuasion, that is, a means used to dissuade an army from opening fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: I really don't know what thoughts went through the minds of the people who did that. I don't know whether it was to prevent people from shooting or to -- us take the bullets. It could have been one of the reasons, at least this is what I heard later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague just asked me if the witness could clarify that there are a number of war criminals who still have not been persecuted. Was he referring to persons of all ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS XX
utterances.text: Of course I was referring to persons of all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for coming here to give us testimony. We wish you good luck in your future. The usher may take you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender two exhibits for this witness. First one is Exhibit 14.5/10. The other exhibit is Exhibit 11.18/8 under seal, the second, the 11.18/8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Those two documents will be admitted into evidence under seal. Mr. Scott, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We've, I think quite pleasantly, ended a bit early, but actually it would give me the time, if the Chamber will allow, to address some of these other matters and then we can start with the next witness first thing in the morning. Your Honour, concerning -- I was looking for the pseudonym of the one witness. If I could just have one moment, I'm about to get it. Your Honour, concerning the request the Chamber made for statements concerning a witness who -- it was Witness QQ, there was an incident in the courtroom, and Your Honour, Mr. President, you directed that an inquiry be made into that. I have provided that -- those statements to counsel already, just this afternoon, but I also will tender -- I will also tender three copies, Your Honours, to the Judges and one copy for the Registrar. Obviously, these will have to be filed under seal, but I expect this is what the Chamber requested. I'm assuming that you wanted these to be provided not only to counsel but to the Court. So that's the -- I'm operating on that assumption. And again, for the record, this is concerning Witness QQ and should be received under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could Madam Registrar give a number to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just provided -- perhaps for identification purposes. We are not making it an exhibit. And again, Mr. President, I guess I'm looking -- perhaps if I'm doing something contrary to what the Court intended, but I thought -- this is what I contemplated the Chamber had asked us, to take this statement and provide it to the Chamber. We don't -- we are not tendering it as evidence as such but simply making a report back to the Chamber, on your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know at least it should have an ID number so that we could find those documents in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. President. Secondly, Your Honours, I can also tender now to Your Honours and to counsel -- and again I'm operating on the same assumptions. This is not evidence, but to respond to the Court's direction, I can now provide statements from Witness -- follow-up statements concerning Witness PP, which I will tender at this time and should be again, please, placed under seal. As soon as these have been distributed, I'll make a few comments, but I'll deal with the distribution first. Counsel -- I think counsel -- no, counsel needs them as well. I'll say, for purposes of the translation booth, I don't think it will be necessary -- I don't think anyone is going to be making extensive reference to these documents that we are now distributing at this time, but if it becomes necessary, I will. I'm also tendering, Mr. President, the supplemental statement of Witness OO, which again should be, please, received under seal. In fact, I believe, if I'm not mistaken, concerning Witness OO, there are two statements. I should also state for the record, B/C/S versions have also been provided. But I think with Witness OO, there are actually two statements stapled together as one packet, but there are two related items on that, so there is no confusion. And then finally, Your Honours, I'm happy to tender to Your Honours and to counsel a set of photographs, and again ask that these be marked, at the moment only for identification, as are the -- as the other statements as well, the statements that we've just handed out. Mr. President, and again for the Witness PP statements and the Witness OO statements, I think, to be consistent, I agree, Mr. President, they should also be given numbers just for identification. At the moment, Mr. President, I'm tendering these, again, the photo -- what's been -- the packet that has the photos can again be made -- be given an identification number for now. One of the things I'll ask the Chamber, if the Chamber cares to give me guidance, I suppose you don't have to, but Chamber might care to give us some additional guidance as to what its thinking is on this matter, and I can give a further report at the moment, but I was just dealing with all the procedural regularities first. But the photo album consists of a number of photographs, and let me say that the investigation so far -- and I realise, fully realise, that what I'm about -- what I'm saying is not evidence, of course, and I don't mean to suggest it is. I'm simply making a report to the Chamber on the investigation that I understand the Chamber directed us to undertake. This is not the rifle -- we do not believe in the investigation so far that this is the rifle that was referenced by Witness OO. I'm sorry if this gets a bit confusing, but I'll try to make it as simple as possible. We do not believe so far that this is the rifle that had been associated with Witness OO. We submit that it is likely - but again not -- we are not certain - that it is likely a rifle associated with the Witness PP. You will see that, as it's been described by various witnesses, if the Chamber has the photographs out of the packet, there are different views of the rifle. I won't go through all of them individually. There are some, looking at the photograph, next to a person showing their leg, to give the Chamber some scale, both sides of the rifle. There is one photograph with the rifle turned, if you will, to show its thinnest dimension, the narrow -- showing the width or thickness of the rifle, I suppose. And others showing different portions of the rifle. I'll just stop on two -- the two, I think, toward the end. The Chamber will have this version on which various markings have been placed which shows the dimensions of the rifle, and on this larger version, you will have then the rifle on both sides. Based on the inquiries that have been made so far, Mr. President, this does not appear to be a rifle that -- there was a reference to a rifle being in a museum. We do not believe that that is this rifle. But subsequent to the matter coming up in court, the inquiries were made and this rifle was found, which we submit, we think, on the current information available to us, is likely the rifle associated with Witness PP. Now, as I said, I don't know exactly what the Chamber's views might be, in terms of what -- where it would like to go with this in terms of witnesses being recalled or further inquiries being made, and I'm not suggesting that you need to give me any additional guidance this evening, or at all for that matter. Of course, I'm in the Chamber's hands, but, Your Honour, I wanted to report that the Prosecution had sought to fulfil the instructions that you gave us and have made this report to you and Your Honour Judge Clark and Your Honour Judge Diarra. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We believe that you made great efforts in this respect. But the one question I want to ask before Mr. Seric, whether you have made any efforts to get that rifle in the museum yet, because that wooden rifle was specifically mentioned by that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer is yes, but we've not been able to locate it at this point. Not sure that it's still where it once -- people once thought it was, but we are still making additional inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Based on the words that you used when you addressed the Prosecutor, I see that we are on the same wavelength. That is precisely what I was about to say, that the rifle, this rifle, which was one of the elements on which we could verify the statement of this witness, should have been here and should have been in that museum beforehand, as you very accurately put it, Mr. President. So if -- we want to see that rifle, if that is the rifle that is specifically mentioned by this witness, we want to be able to analyse it, and we would like to have that rifle be tendered into evidence in a proper way, through this proper witness or a proper statement, and we also want to be able to properly cross-examine this witness or statement on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour. These are supplemental statements, and all these statements, in the view of the Defence, cannot be entered into evidence before they have been properly tested, verified, in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I understand, the Prosecutor has no intention to tender these into the evidence at this stage. They just act in accordance with orders from this Trial Chamber. The purpose for giving each a number is just for the identification. They are not the evidence, at least at this moment. Having said that, Madam Registrar will give a proper number, that is the ID number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. The first statement, which is statement of QQ, will be ID 3. The next statement, which is statement of PP, is ID 4. Under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under seal. The next statement of OO is ID 5, and that also is under seal. The series of photographs are as follows: The first page which describes the rifles, which is document number 02132831, is ID 6. The next exhibit, which is PB-KA-01, is marked as ID 6.1. utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 9.30.
